name: ACE inhibitors, ARBs and amlodipine compared
headline: ACE inhibitors, ARBs and calcium-channel blockers: how do they differ?
summary: ARBs work much like ACE inhibitors but do not cause the dry cough; amlodipine relaxes artery walls differently and can swell ankles.
keyPoints: The NHS says younger adults and people with type 2 diabetes are usually offered an ACE inhibitor or ARB first, and others a calcium-channel blocker.
A persistent dry cough is the best-known side effect of ACE inhibitors such as ramipril and lisinopril, and ARBs such as losartan are a common alternative.
Swollen ankles, feet and legs are a common side effect of the calcium-channel blocker amlodipine.
ACE inhibitors and ARBs need blood tests for kidney function and potassium, and are not normally recommended in pregnancy.
Pharmacists and GPs can advise on side effects and missed doses; the NHS says to call 999 for a serious allergic reaction with swelling of the throat or tongue.

body.heading: What do these medicines do?
body.body: The NHS lists ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) and calcium-channel blockers among the main medicines used to lower high blood pressure. Ramipril and lisinopril are ACE inhibitors, losartan is an ARB, and amlodipine is a calcium-channel blocker. The British Heart Foundation says ACE inhibitors reduce a hormone that narrows blood vessels, so the vessels widen and relax. This lowers blood pressure and improves blood flow to the heart. It says ARBs work in a similar way to ACE inhibitors. Calcium-channel blockers relax the muscle in the artery walls, which widens the arteries and lowers blood pressure. The NHS says amlodipine treats high blood pressure and also angina, a type of chest pain. The NHS says losartan is also used in heart failure and to protect the kidneys in diabetic kidney disease.

body.heading: Which type is usually tried first?
body.body: NICE guideline NG136 covers diagnosing and managing high blood pressure in adults. The NHS says younger adults, and adults of any age with type 2 diabetes, are usually offered an ACE inhibitor or an ARB. Older adults, and adults of any age who are of African or Caribbean family origin and do not have type 2 diabetes, are usually offered a calcium-channel blocker. NICE-based guidance says an ACE inhibitor and an ARB should not be combined to treat high blood pressure. It also says an ARB is offered if an ACE inhibitor is not tolerated, for example because of cough. If blood pressure stays high on an ACE inhibitor or ARB, the guidance offers a calcium-channel blocker or a thiazide-like diuretic as the next step. The NHS adds that ARBs are often recommended when ACE inhibitors cause troublesome side effects.

body.heading: What side effects are typical of each?
body.body: For ramipril, the NHS lists a dry, persistent cough as a common side effect. It says cough medicines do not usually help, and that the cough sometimes settles if the medicine is continued. If it does not, the doctor might suggest changing to a different medicine. The British Heart Foundation names cough as the most common side effect of ACE inhibitors, with headaches, dizziness and rash also possible. The NHS says dizziness or light-headedness, especially on standing or sitting up quickly, is more likely when starting ramipril or moving to a higher dose. Because ARBs do not cause the dry cough, they are often prescribed as an alternative. The BHF lists dizziness, headache and tiredness as ARB side effects. The NHS says the main side effects of losartan are feeling dizzy and tired, and that they are usually mild. For amlodipine, the NHS lists swelling in the ankles, feet and legs as a common side effect. Its advice is to raise the legs when sitting, and to talk to a pharmacist or doctor if that does not help. The BHF lists headaches, swollen ankles and constipation for calcium-channel blockers, and says grapefruit juice can raise the risk of side effects with some of them.

body.heading: What about the kidneys and potassium?
body.body: The NHS says a doctor carries out blood tests before ramipril is started, and when the dose changes, to check the kidneys and potassium levels. The BHF says ARBs can affect kidney function, so regular blood tests are needed. It advises avoiding potassium salt substitutes and potassium supplements with ARBs. For ACE inhibitors it advises avoiding anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen. The NHS ramipril page says swollen ankles, blood in the urine or passing no urine can be signs of kidney problems, and advises getting medical help. Swollen ankles therefore have more than one possible cause, and a review of amlodipine-related swelling says anyone concerned about swelling should seek medical advice.

body.heading: What do they mean for pregnancy?
body.body: The NHS says losartan is not normally recommended in pregnancy or while breastfeeding. A UK patient leaflet says it is not recommended in early pregnancy and must not be taken later in pregnancy, because it may seriously harm the baby. A UK ramipril leaflet says a switch to a suitable alternative should happen before a planned pregnancy. NICE-based local guidance says ACE inhibitors and ARBs should not be used in pregnancy, while breastfeeding or when planning pregnancy unless absolutely necessary. For amlodipine, the NHS says it is not usually recommended in pregnancy because similar medicines are considered safer. It may be used if those do not work and the condition needs treating, and the doctor discusses the risks and benefits. The NHS advises telling the doctor about pregnancy or a possible pregnancy.

body.heading: Who can advise about side effects or a missed dose?
body.body: The NHS pages for each medicine give advice on missed doses, and they say not to take a double dose to make up for a forgotten one. A pharmacist or GP can answer non-urgent questions about side effects, and NHS 111 can give urgent advice. The NHS says to call 999 for a serious allergic reaction, with signs such as a swollen throat or tongue and difficulty breathing. The NHS lists angio-oedema, which is swelling of the lips, tongue and face, among the serious side effects of lisinopril. The BHF says to talk to a doctor before stopping or changing any medicine. This guide describes what the sources say and does not replace advice from the person who prescribes the medicine.
